claim: Command-like descending neurons can induce many behaviors, such as backward locomotion, escape, feeding, courtship, egg-laying, or grooming.
source: Command-like descending neurons can induce many behaviors, such as backward locomotion, escape, feeding, courtship, egg-laying, or grooming (we define 'command-like neuron' as a neuron whose activation elicits or 'commands' a specific behavior).
evidence: The claim is supported by the statement in the abstract, which provides a definition and examples of command-like neurons.

claim: A bilateral pair of Drosophila larval 'mooncrawler descending neurons' (MDNs) have command-like ability to coordinately induce backward locomotion and block forward locomotion.
source: Here, we use genetic screens, intersectional genetics, circuit reconstruction by electron microscopy, and functional optogenetics to identify a bilateral pair of Drosophila larval 'mooncrawler descending neurons' (MDNs) with command-like ability to coordinately induce backward locomotion and block forward locomotion
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: MDNs induce backward locomotion by stimulating a backward-active premotor neuron.
source: the former by stimulating a backward-active premotor neuron
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing MDN activation of A18b neurons.

claim: MDNs block forward locomotion by disynaptic inhibition of a forward-specific premotor neuron.
source: and the latter by disynaptic inhibition of a forward-specific premotor neuron
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by connectomic and functional data showing the MDN-Pair1-A27h pathway.

claim: Direct monosynaptic reciprocal inhibition between forward and backward circuits was not observed.
source: In contrast, direct monosynaptic reciprocal inhibition between forward and backward circuits was not observed.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by connectomic analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Larval MDNs persist into adulthood.
source: Interestingly, larval MDNs persist into adulthood, where they can trigger backward walking.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by immortalization experiments and morphological analysis in Figures 8.

claim: Adult MDNs can trigger backward walking.
source: Interestingly, larval MDNs persist into adulthood, where they can trigger backward walking.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic activation experiments in adult flies shown in Figure 8.

claim: MDNs induce backward locomotion in both limbless and limbed animals.
source: Thus, MDNs induce backward locomotion in both limbless and limbed animals.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral experiments in larvae (limbless) and adults (limbed).

claim: Animals typically execute one behavior to the exclusion of all other possible behaviors.
source: Animals typically execute one behavior to the exclusion of all other possible behaviors (Briggman and Kristan, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Leeches can either crawl or swim, but cannot do both simultaneously.
source: For example, leeches can either crawl or swim, but cannot do both simultaneously (Briggman and Kristan, 2006; Kristan, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on leech behavior.

claim: A locust is capable of either walking or flying but cannot execute both behaviors at the same time.
source: or using the same set of muscles, a locust is capable of either walking or flying but cannot execute both behaviors at the same time (Ramirez and Pearson, 1988)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work on locust behavior.

claim: Mutually exclusive choice of behavior has been observed in several systems, including C. elegans, Tritonia, leech, tadpole, turtle, and zebrafish.
source: Such mutually exclusive choice of behavior has also been observed in several other systems, including Caenorhabditis elegans (forward vs backward crawling), Tritonia (crawling vs swimming), leech (feeding vs swimming), tadpole (struggling vs swimming), turtle (swimming vs scratching), and zebrafish (left vs right escape) (Berkowitz, 2002; Gaudry and Kristan, 2010; Koyama et al., 2016; Popescu and Frost, 2002; Roberts et al., 2016; Soffe, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work on various animal systems.

claim: The selection of a locomotor program to the exclusion of all others is necessary to prevent injury and escape predation.
source: The selection of a locomotor program to the exclusion of all others is necessary to prevent injury and escape predation.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the functional importance of mutually exclusive behaviors.

claim: The underlying circuitry for rapid transitions between antagonistic motor programs is only beginning to be understood in C. elegans.
source: Despite the paramount importance of rapid transitions between antagonistic motor programs, the underlying circuitry is only beginning to be understood in C. elegans (Lindsay et al., 2011; Piggott et al., 2011; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent work on C. elegans circuits.

claim: Command-like neurons can elicit specific behaviors, such as forward locomotion, backward locomotion, pausing, escape, flight, grooming, feeding, courtship, egg-laying or sleep.
source: Command-like neurons can elicit specific behaviors, such as forward locomotion, backward locomotion, pausing, escape, flight, grooming, feeding, courtship, egg-laying or sleep (Bidaye et al., 2014; Bouvier et al., 2015; Hägglund et al., 2010; Hampel et al., 2015; Hedwig, 2000; Hückesfeld et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015; Liu and Fetcho, 1999; Ohyama et al., 2015; Pearson et al., 1985; Sen et al., 2017; Tanouye and Wyman, 1980; von Philipsborn et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work on command-like neurons.

claim: Much less is known about how antagonistic motor programs are suppressed during command neuron-induced behavior.
source: However, much less is known about how antagonistic motor programs are suppressed during command neuron-induced behavior.
evidence: The claim reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Forward locomotion is the default locomotor behavior in Drosophila larvae.
source: Drosophila larva have many distinct behaviors (Vogelstein et al., 2014), but forward locomotion is the default locomotor behavior (Berni et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Forward locomotion in Drosophila larvae consists of coordinated posterior-to-anterior waves of somatic body wall muscle contractions driven by corresponding waves of motor neuron activity within the segmented ventral nerve cord.
source: and consists of coordinated posterior-to-anterior waves of somatic body wall muscle contractions driven by corresponding waves of motor neuron activity within the segmented ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Clark et al., 2018; Heckscher et al., 2012; Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Pulver et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work on larval locomotion.

claim: There are approximately 35 motor neurons per bilateral hemisegment in Drosophila larvae.
source: There are ~35 motor neurons per bilateral hemisegment, innervating 30 body wall muscles (Landgraf and Thor, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: There are 30 body wall muscles per bilateral hemisegment in Drosophila larvae.
source: There are ~35 motor neurons per bilateral hemisegment, innervating 30 body wall muscles (Landgraf and Thor, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: There are about 250 interneurons per hemisegment in Drosophila larvae.
source: about 250 interneurons per hemisegment (Rickert et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: Larvae initiate backward locomotion upon encountering a barrier or experiencing mild noxious stimulation to the anterior body.
source: Larvae initiate backward locomotion upon encountering a barrier or experiencing mild noxious stimulation to the anterior body (Kernan et al., 1994; Robertson et al., 2013; Takagi et al., 2017; Titlow et al., 2014; Tracey et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Backward locomotion consists of anterior-to-posterior waves of motor neuron and muscle activity.
source: Backward locomotion consists of anterior-to-posterior waves of motor neuron and muscle activity (Heckscher et al., 2012; Pulver et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on backward locomotion.

claim: A segmentally reiterated VNC neuron that triggers backward locomotion has been identified.
source: A segmentally reiterated VNC neuron that triggers backward locomotion has been identified (Takagi et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: High-order command-like neurons for backward locomotion remain unknown.
source: but high-order command-like neurons for backward locomotion and the circuit for executing backward wave propagation while simultaneously suppressing forward waves remain unknown.
evidence: The claim reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The circuit for executing backward wave propagation while simultaneously suppressing forward waves remains unknown.
source: but high-order command-like neurons for backward locomotion and the circuit for executing backward wave propagation while simultaneously suppressing forward waves remain unknown.
evidence: The claim reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The only neurons present in all three Split lines (Split1, Split2, and Split3) are a bilateral pair of neurons with cell bodies located in the ventral, anterior, medial brain with descending processes to A3-A5 in the VNC.
source: We identified three lines called Split1, Split2, and Split3 labeling different subsets of the original pattern; the only neurons present in all three Split lines are a bilateral pair of neurons with cell bodies located in the ventral, anterior, medial brain with descending processes to A3-A5 in the VNC (Figure 1A–C, arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: All three Split lines could induce backward locomotion following Chrimson expression and activation.
source: All three Split lines could induce backward locomotion following Chrimson expression and activation (Figure 1D, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1D and Videos 1-2.

claim: Neuronal activation immediately switched locomotion from forward to backward.
source: Neuronal activation immediately switched locomotion from forward to backward (Figure 1E,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: There was no significant change in the number of peristaltic waves per second following MDN activation.
source: without a significant change in the number of peristaltic waves per second (Split1, 0.48; Split2, 0.50; Split3, 0.65 before activation; Split1, 0.48; Split2, 0.56; Split3, 0.56 after activation).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data.

claim: Using Split2 or Split3 to express GtACR1 significantly reduced backward locomotion induced by a noxious head poke.
source: Conversely, using Split2 or Split3 to express the light-inducible neuronal silencer GtACR1 (Mohammad et al., 2017) significantly reduced backward locomotion induced by a noxious head poke (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic silencing experiments shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: All larvae with a backward locomotion phenotype expressed Chrimson:Venus in one or both neurons from the anterior, medial pair that had descending projections to A3-A5.
source: All larvae with a backward locomotion phenotype (n = 10) expressed Chrimson:Venus in one or both neurons from the anterior, medial pair that had descending projections to A3-A5 (three examples shown in Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by stochastic labeling experiments shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: All larvae that lacked Chrimson-induced backward locomotion never showed Chrimson:Venus expression in the ventral, anterior, medial descending neurons.
source: Conversely, all larvae that lacked Chrimson-induced backward locomotion (n = 20) never showed Chrimson:Venus expression in the ventral, anterior, medial descending neurons (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data from stochastic labeling experiments.

claim: MDNs are cholinergic.
source: The MDNs are likely to be excitatory, as they are cholinergic (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChAT:GFP expression data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Activation of as few as two of the four MDNs is sufficient to induce a behavioral switch from forward to backward locomotion.
source: We conclude that activation of as few as two of the four MDNs (either both in the same brain lobe or one in each brain lobe) is sufficient to induce a behavioral switch from forward to backward locomotion.
evidence: The claim is based on the stochastic labeling experiments showing that larvae with one or both MDNs labeled exhibit backward locomotion.

claim: MDNs are active during backward but not forward locomotion.
source: We detected little or no activity-induced red fluorescence during forward locomotion, but significant red fluorescence during backward locomotion (Figure 2G). We conclude that MDNs are active during backward but not forward locomotion.
evidence: The claim is supported by CaMPARI experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Two neurons indistinguishable from the MDNs can be identified in the TEM reconstruction.
source: We found two pair of neurons that showed an excellent morphological match to the MDNs in every distinctive feature (Figure 3A'–D'); we annotate them as MDNa and MDNb in the TEM volume.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological matching between light microscopy and TEM shown in Figure 3.

claim: MDN pre-synapses are restricted to the descending processes.
source: Pre-synapses are restricted to the descending processes (Figure 4A, green)
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM reconstruction data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MDN post-synapses are present in brain arbors and descending processes.
source: whereas post-synapses are present in brain arbors and descending processes, suggesting information flow from brain to VNC.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM reconstruction data.

claim: MDN output synapses are polyadic.
source: A representative MDN output synapse shown in Figure 4B; it is polyadic (multiple postsynaptic neurons clustered around the MDN pre-synapse) and electron dense with associated presynaptic vesicles.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The post-synaptic partners with the most synapses with MDN are: (1) the Pair1 SEZ descending neuron; (2) the thoracic descending neuron (ThDN); (3) the premotor neuron A18b; and (4) the MDNs themselves.
source: The post-synaptic partners with the most synapses with MDN are: (1) the Pair1 SEZ descending neuron; (2) the thoracic descending neuron (ThDN); (3) the premotor neuron A18b; and (4) the MDNs themselves (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectomic analysis shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: All four MDNs have similar connectivity.
source: All four MDNs have similar connectivity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ThDN has a large number of synapses with A27l/A27k premotor neurons.
source: For example, ThDN has a large number of synapses with A27l/A27k premotor neurons (Figure 4C,E,H)
evidence: The claim is supported by connectomic data shown in Figure 4C,E,H.

claim: Pair1 is connected to the premotor neuron A27h, both directly and indirectly.
source: Pair1 is connected to the previously described premotor neuron A27h (Fushiki et al., 2016), both directly and indirectly (Figure 4C,F,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectomic data shown in Figure 4C,F,J and a citation to previous work.

claim: A18b is a premotor neuron present in all abdominal segments, but it only receives MDN input in segment A1.
source: Lastly, A18b is a premotor neuron present in all abdominal segments, but it only receives MDN input in segment A1 (Figure 4C,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectomic data shown in Figure 4C,I.

claim: A18b is cholinergic.
source: is cholinergic (Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChAT:GFP expression data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A18b is connected directly to the dorsal-projecting motor neurons aCC/RP2 and U1/U2.
source: and is connected directly to the dorsal-projecting motor neurons aCC/RP2 and U1/U2 (Figure 5C) among other motor neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by connectomic data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In fictive preparations, A18b neurons are active in backward but not forward locomotion.
source: In fictive preparations, A18b neurons are active in backward but not forward locomotion. ΔF/F0 of GCaMP6m in U1-U5 motor neurons (top) or jRCaMP1b in A18b (bottom) of five segments executing a forward (FWD) and then a backward (BWD) wave. This experiment was performed on eight different isolated third instar CNSs with similar results; quantified in E.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: In intact larvae, A18b neurons are active in backward but not forward locomotion.
source: In intact larvae, A18b neurons are active in backward but not forward locomotion. ΔF/F0 of GCaMP6m in motor neurons (top) and jRCaMP1b in A18b (bottom) in three segments. Times of BWD and FWD motor waves indicated. This experiment was performed on 19 waves (11 BWD, 8 FWD) in seven third instar larvae, all with similar results; quantified in E.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5D',E.

claim: In intact larvae, A18b is preferentially active during backward not forward locomotion.
source: In intact larvae, A18b is preferentially active during backward not forward locomotion. CaMPARI in A18b neurites in a third instar larval CNS.
evidence: The claim is supported by CaMPARI experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: MDNs activate A18b neurons.
source: To determine if MDNs activate A18b, we used Split1 to express Chrimson in MDNs and A18b-lexA to express GCaMP6f in A18b in fictive preparations. MDN stimulation led to a significant increase in GCaMP6f fluorescence in A18b, and this was not observed in controls lacking all-trans retinal (ATR), an essential co-factor for Chrimson function (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation and calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 5G.

claim: MDN activation triggered a backward wave of A18b activity from A2 to A6.
source: Interestingly, MDN activation triggered a backward wave of A18b activity from A2 to A6 (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A18b and motor neurons are co-active during backward waves.
source: we observed co-activity of A18b and motor neurons during backward motor waves in fictive preparation (Figure 5H)
evidence: The claim is supported by dual-color calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: A18b stimulation led to a significant increase in GCaMP6f fluorescence in motor neurons.
source: and A18b stimulation led to a significant increase in GCaMP6f fluorescence in motor neurons, which was not observed in controls lacking ATR (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation and calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 5I.

claim: MDNs activate Pair1 neurons.
source: To determine if MDNs activate Pair1 we used Split1 to express Chrimson in MDNs, and R75C02-lexA (hereafter Pair1-lexA) (Figure 6A) to express GCaMP6f specifically in Pair1. Stimulation of MDNs led to a significant increase in Pair1 GCaMP6f fluorescence, and this was not observed in controls lacking ATR (Figure 6B). We conclude that the MDNs activate Pair1 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation and calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Every time MDNs were active, the Pair1 neurons were co-active.
source: In addition, we observed that every time MDNs were active, the Pair1 neurons were co-active (n = 5; Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Pair1 could be active alone.
source: although Pair1 could be active alone (n = 5; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pair1 is active during backward but not forward waves in fictive preparations.
source: Pair1 is active during backward (BWD) but not forward (FWD) waves in fictive preparations. Left: Pair1 GCaMP6m activity (bottom) and motor neuron activity (top) during fictive BWD and FWD waves in the same animal. Pair1 is not active during FWD waves.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pair1 activity precedes motor neuron activity.
source: In cases where Pair1 activity is coupled with motor neuron activity, we find that Pair1 activity precedes motor neuron activity (Figure 6D, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pair1 is preferentially active during backward locomotion in the intact animal.
source: Pair1 is preferentially active during backward locomotion in the intact animal. CaMPARI was expressed in Pair1 and photoconversion was activated during FWD or BWD locomotion in intact third instar larvae. There is significantly more CaMPARI photoconversion during BWD locomotion.
evidence: The claim is supported by CaMPARI experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A27h is active during forward not backward locomotion.
source: We confirm previous work (Fushiki et al., 2016) showing that A27h is active during forward not backward locomotion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and a citation to previous work.

claim: Pair1 inhibits the A27h neuron.
source: To test whether Pair1 inhibits the A27h neuron, we expressed Chrimson in Pair1 and GCaMP6m in A27h. We used Chrimson to stimulate Pair1 just as A27h activity was rising as part of a forward motor wave, and observed a significant decrease in A27h GCaMP6m fluorescence; this was not observed in controls lacking ATR (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation and calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Pair1 neurons are GABAergic.
source: Furthermore, we found that Pair1 neurons are GABAergic (Figure 7A''), consistent with Pair1 direct repression of A27h activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by GABA immunostaining shown in Figure 7A''.

claim: Chrimson stimulation of Pair1 immediately and persistently blocked forward larval locomotion.
source: In addition, we found that Chrimson stimulation of Pair1 immediately and persistently blocked forward larval locomotion; control larvae lacking ATR briefly paused in response to illumination onset but rapidly resumed forward locomotion (Figure 7C; Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7C and Videos 3-4.

claim: Pair1 and A27h activity is anti-correlated.
source: Consistent with an inhibitory relationship, we observed that Pair1 and A27h activity is anti-correlated, with A27h often rising in activity as Pair1 declines in activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Silencing Pair1 alone had no effect on forward locomotion.
source: We observed that silencing Pair1 alone had no effect on forward locomotion (Figure 7E,i–ii)
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic silencing experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Silencing Pair1 prior to MDN activation led to a loss in the effectiveness of MDN-induced backward locomotion.
source: but silencing Pair1 prior to low light or high light Chrimson-induced activation of MDN led to a loss in the effectiveness of MDN-induced backward locomotion (Figure 7E,iii–vi).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Larval MDNs share several features with the moonwalker descending neurons characterized in the adult.
source: Larval MDNs share several features with the moonwalker descending neurons characterized in the adult (Bidaye et al., 2014; Sen et al., 2017). Both larval and adult neurons have anterior, medial somata with ipsilateral and contralateral arbors, and descending projections into the VNC. Both have presynaptic output into the SEZ and VNC.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological comparison and citations to previous work on adult moonwalker neurons.

claim: MDNs were observed at early pupal stages.
source: We tried to trace the MDNs through pupal stages using the Split1-Gal4 and observed the MDNs at early pupal stages (Figure 8A)
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: MDNs began to prune their dendritic arbors at mid-pupal stages.
source: and mid-pupal stages, where they began to prune their dendritic arbors (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Light activation of immortalized larval MDNs induced backward walking in 8 of 10 adult flies assayed.
source: We observed light-induced backward walking in 8 of 10 adult flies assayed (Figure 8D; Video 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments shown in Figure 8D and Video 5.

claim: All eight flies that walked backward had ReaChr::citrine expression in neurons matching the moonwalker neuron morphology.
source: all eight had ReaChr::citrine expression in neurons matching the moonwalker neuron morphology (Figure 8E,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: The two flies that did not walk backward did not have ReaChr:citrine expression in moonwalker neurons.
source: whereas the two flies that did not walk backward also did not have ReaChr:citrine expression in moonwalker neurons (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data from the immortalization experiments.

claim: All backward walking adults that were successfully stained showed expression in the adult moonwalker neurons.
source: Importantly, all the backward walking adults that were successfully stained showed expression in the adult moonwalker neurons (n = 5; Figure 8I,I')
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis shown in Figure 8I,I'.

claim: The larval MDNs are descending neurons that are born embryonically, persist throughout larval stages, and survive into the adult.
source: We conclude that the larval MDNs are descending neurons that are born embryonically, persist throughout larval stages, and survive into the adult.
evidence: The claim is based on the immortalization experiments and morphological analysis throughout development.

claim: Activation of MDNs can induce backward crawling in the limbless larva, as well as backward walking in the six-limbed adult.
source: Surprisingly, activation of MDNs can induce backward crawling in the limbless larva, as well as backward walking in the six-limbed adult (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic behavioral experiments in larvae and adults.

claim: MDNs are brain descending interneurons that activate two neuronal pathways: one to stop forward locomotion and one to induce backward locomotion.
source: We have shown that MDNs are brain descending interneurons that activate two neuronal pathways: one to stop forward locomotion and one to induce backward locomotion (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: In C. elegans, in response to a head poke the ASH sensory neuron activates AVA, a command neuron for backward locomotion.
source: This is similar to C. elegans, where in response to a head poke the ASH sensory neuron activates AVA, a command neuron for backward locomotion (Lindsay et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work on C. elegans.

claim: In C. elegans, ASH indirectly inhibits AVB, a command neuron for forward locomotion.
source: and indirectly inhibits AVB, a command neuron for forward locomotion (Roberts et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work on C. elegans.

claim: AVB inhibition in C. elegans may also arise from reciprocal inhibition between AVA and AVB.
source: although AVB inhibition may also arise from reciprocal inhibition between AVA and AVB.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about alternative mechanisms in C. elegans.

claim: MDNs can induce backward locomotion within intact larvae or isolated CNS.
source: MDNs can induce backward locomotion within intact larvae or isolated CNS.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experiments in both preparations.

claim: A pulse of Chrimson activation as short as 300 ms can induce a full, multi-second long backward wave.
source: In each case, a pulse of Chrimson activation as short as 300 ms can induce a full, multi-second long backward wave, suggesting that MDN activity triggers a backward wave without persisting throughout the wave.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: MDN activity triggers but does not persist throughout a backward wave.
source: suggesting that MDN activity triggers a backward wave without persisting throughout the wave. These results are consistent with detection of MDN-A18b synapses only in segment A1, and support our conclusion that MDNs trigger but do not persist throughout, a backward wave.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from optogenetic and connectomic data.

claim: Noxious stimuli that produce multiple waves of backward locomotion are likely to continuously activate MDNs.
source: Noxious stimuli that produce multiple waves of backward locomotion are likely to continuously activate MDNs.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about how sustained backward locomotion is maintained.

claim: MDNs are necessary for a normal backward locomotor response following mild noxious touch to the head.
source: MDNs are necessary for a normal backward locomotor response following mild noxious touch to the head.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic silencing experiments shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: There are no monosynaptic sensory inputs to the MDNs in the current TEM connectome.
source: It is unclear how the tactile sensory cue is transduced to the MDNs: we find no monosynaptic sensory inputs to the MDNs in the current TEM connectome (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on connectomic analysis.

claim: It is unknown whether MDNs are used for backward crawling in response to other noxious sensory modalities, such as high salt, bright light, or bitter taste.
source: It is also unknown whether MDNs are used for backward crawling in response to other noxious sensory modalities, such as high salt, bright light, or bitter taste.
evidence: The claim reflects the current limitations of the study.

claim: MDNs may be dedicated to responding to noxious mechanosensation, or they may integrate multimodal inputs to initiate backward locomotion.
source: MDNs may be dedicated to responding to noxious mechanosensation, or they may integrate multimodal inputs to initiate backward locomotion.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about MDN function.

claim: A descending command-like neuron that induces forward locomotion is likely to project into the posterior abdominal segments, where forward waves are initiated.
source: Whereas the MDN descending projection extends to A3-A5, and thus well past the thoracic and upper abdominal segments that initiate backward locomotion (Berni, 2015; Heckscher et al., 2012; Pulver et al., 2015), a descending command-like neuron that induces forward locomotion is likely to project into the posterior abdominal segments, where forward waves are initiated (Berni, 2015; Heckscher et al., 2012; Pulver et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known sites of forward wave initiation and citations to previous work.

claim: The model is that the activation of A18b in A1 induces backward locomotion.
source: Our model is that the activation of A18b in A1 induces backward locomotion. This model is based on several observations. (1) A18b is only active during backward locomotion. (2) MDN forms excitatory synapses on A18b in A1 but not more posterior segments. (3) Stimulation of MDN produces an A18b backward activity wave. (4) The A18b backward wave is always concurrent with a motor neuron backward wave.
evidence: The claim is based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Backward motor waves are initiated from the thorax.
source: Backward motor waves are initiated from the thorax (Pulver et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: There are additional mechanisms to induce Pair1 activity, as many Pair1 activity bouts occur without MDN activity.
source: But there are also additional mechanisms to induce Pair1 activity, as many Pair1 activity bouts occur without MDN activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MDN-independent inputs that activate Pair1 remain to be discovered.
source: The MDN-independent inputs that activate Pair1 remain to be discovered.
evidence: The claim reflects the current limitations of the study.

claim: There are currently no genetic tools providing access to ThDN or A27k neurons.
source: There are currently no genetic tools providing access to ThDN or A27k neurons, and the existing driver line for A27l has off-target neurons, precluding a functional analysis of this pathway.
evidence: The claim reflects the current technical limitations.

claim: Most mechanosensory neurons are completely different between larva and adult.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Most or all the downstream motor neurons controlling crawling (larva) and walking (adult) are different: abdominal motor neurons in the larva and thoracic motor neurons in the adult.
source: Similarly, most or all the downstream motor neurons controlling crawling (larva) and walking (adult) are different: abdominal motor neurons in the larva and thoracic motor neurons in the adult.
